north-dakota.name: North Dakota
north-dakota._source: North Dakota Office of State Tax Commissioner, 2026 Form ND-1ES (SFN 28709, revised 12-2025), '2026 Forms ND-1 and ND-EZ Tax Rate Schedules': no tax on North Dakota taxable income up to $49,575 single, $82,800 married filing jointly, $66,400 head of household, then 1.95%, then 2.50% above $250,400 single, $304,850 married filing jointly, $277,600 head of household. district-of-columbia.name: District of Columbia

_watch.what: DC's decoupled standard deduction rests on temporary D.C. Law 26-89, scheduled to lapse 2026-09-25, disapproved by Congress (Pub. L. 119-78), with the DC attorney general's opinion scoped to the 2025 filing season. Re-verify: did the act lapse, get made permanent, or did a court rule? If it lapsed, standardDeduction moves to the federal 2026 set and the disclaimers change.
_watch.decided: Edmond 2026-07-31: keep the decoupled amounts until then.

district-of-columbia._source: Rates are the District's schedule of seven brackets, 4% to 10.75%, with the same thresholds for every filing status, set by D.C. Code 47-1806.03(a)(11). The District does not use the federal standard deduction. It sets its own: $15,000 for a single filer or married filing separately, $22,500 for head of household, and $30,000 for a married couple filing jointly, under D.C. Code 47-1801.04(3A). Those are the tax year 2025 amounts. The same figures carry into 2026 subject to a cost-of-living adjustment the District has not published yet, so the 2025 amounts are shown. Filers aged 65 or older or blind may claim an additional standard deduction, which this calculator does not include. Sources: https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/47-1801.04 and https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/47-1806.03 CONGRESSIONAL DISAPPROVAL, as of 2026-07-31: the District's own standard deduction comes from the D.C. Income and Franchise Tax Conformity and Revision Temporary Amendment Act of 2025 (D.C. Act 26-217), which took effect as D.C. Law 26-89 on 2026-02-12 and added the basic standard deduction at D.C. Code 47-1801.04(3A), $15,000 single, $22,500 head of household and $30,000 joint. Congress then disapproved that act by H.J. Res. 142, which the President signed on 2026-02-18 as Public Law 119-78. The two sides disagree about the effect. The District has not changed course: D.C. Code 47-1801.04(3A) still carries those amounts, with a note that the temporary legislation expires 2026-09-25 and no reference to the disapproval, and the Office of Tax and Revenue's 2025 D-40 booklet still instructs taxpayers to use them. The District's attorney general issued an opinion on 2026-02-24 (https://oag.dc.gov/sites/default/files/2026-02/AG-Opinion-Decoupling-Retroactivity-and-Validity-.pdf) concluding that the temporary act remains in effect through the 2025 filing season, while expecting calendar year 2026 taxes not to be governed by it once it lapses. No court has ruled. This page follows what the District is administering and says so on the page. https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-119publ78/html/PLAW-119publ78.htm ; https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/47-1801.04
disclaimer: District income tax. DC uses the same bracket thresholds for all filing statuses.

The District sets its own standard deduction and does not follow the federal amount. The figures used here are the District's tax year 2025 amounts, because DC has not yet published its inflation-adjusted 2026 amounts.
The District's separate standard deduction was created by temporary legislation that is currently scheduled to lapse in late September 2026. If it is not made permanent, the amounts here may change.

Congress voted in February 2026 to undo the DC law behind these amounts. The District's attorney general concluded the vote came too late to block the law and that it remains in effect for the 2025 filing season; the District's tax office is still applying these amounts today, so this page uses them. The disagreement has not been settled.

new-mexico.name: New Mexico
new-mexico._source: New Mexico's 2026 income tax rates come from NMSA 1978, Section 7-2-7, as amended by House Bill 252 (2024 regular session), which sets these six brackets for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2025. Under that section, head of household filers use the same rate table as married couples filing jointly and surviving spouses, not the single table. Standard deduction amounts follow the federal figures for 2026 published by the IRS in Revenue Procedure 2025-32. Statute text: https://www.nmlegis.gov/Sessions/24%20Regular/final/HB0252.pdf
disclaimer: Local income taxes are not included.
New Mexico's $4,000-per-dependent deduction and low/middle-income exemptions are not modeled.
Married filing separately has its own rate table under Section 7-2-7 NMSA 1978 and is not modeled separately.

vermont.name: Vermont
vermont._source: Vermont tax year 2026. BRACKETS for all three filing statuses this page models come from the Vermont Legislative Joint Fiscal Office 2026 Fiscal Facts booklet (issued February 2026), the table on page 50 headed 2026 VERMONT Personal Income Tax Rates and Brackets. Check you are on page 50, because page 49 shows the federal brackets. The four rates are 3.35%, 6.60%, 7.60% and 8.75%, and the table gives single 50,750 / 122,850 / 256,300, married filing jointly 84,700 / 204,750 / 312,050, and head of household 68,000 / 175,500 / 284,150. It also lists married filing separately, which this page does not model. Fiscal Facts is the Legislature's reference publication of current law, not a Department of Taxes schedule: 32 V.S.A. 5822(b)(2) assigns the annual inflation adjustment to the Commissioner of Taxes. It is cited here because it is the only official Vermont document that carries the 2026 brackets today. https://ljfo.vermont.gov/assets/Publications/2026-Fiscal-Facts-Booklet/Fiscal-Facts-2026.pdf STANDARD DEDUCTION figures are Vermont's tax year 2025 amounts, $7,650 single, $15,300 married filing jointly and $11,450 head of household, from the Vermont Department of Taxes 2025 Income Tax Return Booklet, the Form IN-111 Line 4 standard deduction chart. https://tax.vermont.gov/sites/tax/files/documents/Income-Booklet-2025.pdf WHY TWO YEARS: the Department of Taxes has not published 2026 income tax rate schedules or a 2026 standard deduction. The newest schedules on its own rate schedules page are tax year 2025. https://tax.vermont.gov/individuals/personal-income-tax/rates Vermont has published 2026 WITHHOLDING material (GB-1210-2026, RateSched-2026, TaxTables-2026), but those are employer withholding charts covering single and married only, with no head of household column, and their thresholds are not the bracket thresholds, so they are deliberately not cited for any figure on this page.
disclaimer: Local income taxes are not included.
Vermont's per-person personal exemption is not modeled, so this estimate runs slightly high.
The standard deduction shown is Vermont's tax year 2025 amount, because the Department of Taxes has not yet published a tax year 2026 standard deduction.

west-virginia.name: West Virginia
west-virginia._source: WV 2026 schedule after the triggered rate cuts (5 rates 2.22/2.96/3.33/4.44/4.82%, same thresholds for all filing statuses), Tax Foundation as-of Jan 1 2026; cross-check WV Tax Division (tax.wv.gov). WV has NO standard deduction; the $2,000-per-exemption personal exemption is modeled here as the deduction. https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/state/state-income-tax-rates-2026/
disclaimer: Local income taxes are not included. WV municipal service/city fees are not income taxes and are not modeled.
WV has no standard deduction; we model one $2,000 personal exemption ($4,000 MFJ). Each dependent adds another $2,000 not modeled — estimates run slightly high for filers with dependents.
west-virginia.notes: Graduated 2.11% to 4.58% for 2026 after the Senate Bill 392 rate cut, with the same brackets for single, joint and head of household filers.

montana.name: Montana
montana._source: Montana Department of Revenue, 2026 Montana Publication 1, 2026 Tax Tables: 4.7% on the first $47,500 of ordinary income for single filers, $95,000 for married filing jointly, and $71,250 for head of household, then 5.65% above those amounts. Montana starts from federal taxable income, so the standard deduction is the federal amount; the Montana Employer and Information Agent Guide annual withholding tables show it as $16,100 single, $32,200 married filing jointly, and $24,150 head of household. Statute: MCA 15-30-2103. https://revenuefiles.mt.gov/files/Forms/Publication-1/Publication-1-2026.pdf
disclaimer: Local income taxes are not included.
Montana taxes net long-term capital gains at lower rates and has credits not modeled here.

virginia.name: Virginia
virginia._source: VA individual income tax is statutory (Va. Code § 58.1-320), 2%-5.75% at $3k/$5k/$17k thresholds, unchanged since 1990 (same brackets for all filing statuses). Official 2026 standard deduction $8,750 single/HoH, $17,500 MFJ (Va. Code § 58.1-322.03, fixed for 2025-2026). Confirmed against the Va. Dept. of Taxation Tax Rate Schedule (Rev. 05/26); validated vs SmartAsset/Talent.com consensus. https://www.tax.virginia.gov/ ; https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title58.1/chapter3/section58.1-320/
disclaimer: Virginia has no local/city wage income tax.

utah.name: Utah
utah._source: UT flat individual income tax rate 4.45% for tax years beginning on/after Jan 1 2026 (SB60, 2026 General Session, sponsored Sen. McCay/Rep. Eliason; signed by the Governor Mar 23 2026, general effective date May 6 2026 but the rate cut applies retroactively to TY beginning on/after Jan 1 2026; latest in Utah's run of consecutive annual cuts, 4.50%->4.45%, also cutting the corporate/franchise rate 4.50%->4.45% with the $100 minimum unchanged). Utah does NOT tax federal taxable income: TC-40 starts from federal adjusted gross income (line 4, from 1040 line 11), applies Utah additions/subtractions to reach Utah taxable income (line 9), then multiplies by the flat rate (line 10). The federal standard deduction is reflected via the nonrefundable Taxpayer Tax Credit (6% of federal deductions + Utah personal exemptions, phased out at higher income) and a full exemption when FAGI <= the federal standard deduction, NOT by directly reducing the base; this calculator approximates the base as wages minus the federal standard deduction. NOTE: the Utah State Tax Commission rate page (incometax.utah.gov/paying/tax-rates) still lists '4.5% / .045 -- January 1, 2025 -- current' with no 2026 row (a lagging administrative page not yet updated for SB60); the enacted statute controls. https://le.utah.gov/~2026/bills/static/SB0060.html ; https://taxnews.ey.com/news/2026-0913-utah-law-lowers-state-income-tax-rate-retroactive-to-January-1-2026 ; https://orbitax.com/news/country/article/Utah-Cuts-Individual-and-Corpo-61573 ; https://incometax.utah.gov/line-by-line/
disclaimer: Utah's nonrefundable Taxpayer Tax Credit (which phases out with income) is not modeled, so this estimate may overstate tax for lower incomes. Base approximated as wages minus the federal standard deduction.
utah.notes: Flat 4.45% (SB60, TY2026) on Utah taxable income, which starts from federal adjusted gross income adjusted by Utah additions/subtractions (not federal taxable income). The Taxpayer Tax Credit is not modeled; base approximated as wages minus the federal standard deduction.

michigan.name: Michigan
michigan._source: MI flat 4.25%; 2026 personal exemption $5,900 per exemption (MI 2026 Withholding Guide, Form 446). https://www.michigan.gov/treasury

Several Michigan cities (Detroit, Grand Rapids, etc.) levy separate local income taxes not included here.

arizona.name: Arizona
arizona._source: Arizona taxes income at a flat 2.5% (A.R.S. 43-1011). The standard deduction shown is Arizona's published tax year 2025 amount: $15,750 for a single filer or a married person filing separately, $31,500 for a married couple filing jointly, and $23,625 for head of household, read from the Arizona Department of Revenue's 2025 Form 140 instructions. Although A.R.S. 43-1041 states Arizona's own base amounts and indexes them by the federal method, the amounts the Department actually publishes have matched the federal standard deduction, and these three figures are the federal 2025 amounts. Arizona had not published a 2026 standard deduction as of 30 July 2026. Sources: Arizona Department of Revenue 2025 Form 140 instructions, https://azdor.gov/sites/default/files/document/FORMS_INDIVIDUAL_2025_140i.pdf , and A.R.S. 43-1041, https://www.azleg.gov/ars/43/01041.htm
disclaimer: The standard deduction used here is Arizona's published 2025 amount. Arizona releases each year's amount alongside that year's Form 140, and the 2026 amount had not been published as of 30 July 2026.
Arizona also allows an extra standard deduction for charitable contributions if you do not itemize. This calculator does not include it, so your Arizona tax may be slightly lower than shown.
arizona.notes: Flat 2.5% after the AZ standard deduction.

georgia._source: GA flat 4.99% for 2026 (HB 463, signed May 2026, accelerated from 5.19%); standard deduction $15,000 single / $30,000 MFJ. GA Dept. of Revenue. https://dor.georgia.gov/taxes/important-tax-updates

louisiana._source: LA flat 3.0% (Act 11, eff. 2025); 2026 combined standard deduction $12,875 single / $25,750 MFJ & HoH (LA DOR RIB 26-005, Jan 2026). https://revenue.louisiana.gov/
louisiana.notes: Flat 3.0% after the combined standard deduction.

iowa.name: Iowa
iowa._source: IA flat 3.8% for 2026 (Iowa DOR, SF 2442). Iowa conforms to the federal standard deduction. https://revenue.iowa.gov/press-release/2025-10-21/idr-announces-2026-individual-income-tax-and-interest-rates
disclaimer: Iowa's small personal-exemption tax credits ($40 single / $80 MFJ / $40 per dependent) are post-tax credits and are not modeled.

idaho.name: Idaho
idaho._source: Idaho taxes income at a flat 5.3%, and only on taxable income above a zero-rate threshold. Idaho Code 63-3024(2) sets that rate and provides that a head of household return is treated as a joint return, so heads of household use the same threshold as married couples filing jointly (https://legislature.idaho.gov/statutesrules/idstat/Title63/T63CH30/SECT63-3024/). The threshold amounts used here, $4,811 for single filers and $9,622 for joint filers and heads of household, are the 2025 indexed amounts published by the Idaho State Tax Commission (https://tax.idaho.gov/taxes/income-tax/individual-income/individual-income-tax-rate-schedule/), which had not yet published a 2026 schedule. Idaho's standard deduction is the federal standard deduction, because Idaho conforms to the Internal Revenue Code as in effect on January 1, 2026 under House Bill 559 of the 2026 session, Session Law Chapter 1.
idaho.notes: Flat 5.3% on taxable income above a zero-rate threshold: $4,811 for a single filer and $9,622 for a married couple filing jointly or a head of household. Idaho treats a head of household return as a joint return, so both use the same threshold.
disclaimer: Local income taxes are not included.

The zero-rate thresholds used here are Idaho's 2025 inflation-adjusted amounts, because the Idaho State Tax Commission had not published a 2026 rate schedule. Idaho re-indexes them each year, so the 2026 thresholds will be slightly higher and your tax slightly lower than shown.
Idaho charges a $10 Permanent Building Fund tax per return, which this calculator does not include.

ohio.name: Ohio
ohio._source: Ohio 2026 nonbusiness-income tax schedule per the statute as amended by HB 96 (signed June 30, 2025), ORC 5747.02(A)(3): for taxable years beginning in 2026 and thereafter the tax is $332.00 plus 2.75% of the amount in excess of $26,050, i.e. one rate on every taxable dollar above the 0% band. The 3.125% band over $100,000 that HB 96 created was a 2025-only step and does not apply to 2026. Same schedule for all filing statuses. Modeled as marginal brackets (the engine reproduces marginal tax, not Ohio's small base-amount rounding offset). Note the 2026 IT 1040 ES worksheet PDF still prints the superseded pre-HB 96 ladder ($2,394.32 + 3.125% over $100,000); the statute governs. https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-5747.02
disclaimer: Local income taxes are not included. Ohio municipalities and school districts levy separate local income taxes (commonly 1%-3%) that are NOT included in this estimate.
Ohio's $1,900-per-exemption personal/dependent deduction, joint-filing credit, and other credits are not modeled.
ohio.notes: Flat since 2026 (HB 96): 0% up to $26,050, then 2.75% on everything above. Local municipal income taxes not included.

maryland.name: Maryland
maryland._source: Maryland tax year 2026. RATES AND BRACKETS are current for 2026: the Budget Reconciliation and Financing Act of 2025 (House Bill 352, Chapter 604, approved 2025-05-20) set the schedule that applies to tax years beginning after 2024-12-31, keeping the 2% to 5.75% ladder and adding two high-income brackets, 6.25% and 6.5%. Maryland's bracket thresholds are fixed in statute and are not inflation-indexed, so 2026 uses the same thresholds. STANDARD DEDUCTION is the tax year 2025 amount, not a 2026 amount. The same Act rewrote Md. Code, Tax-General 10-217 into flat dollar amounts, $3,350 for a single filer, married filing separately, or a dependent, and $6,700 for a head of household, a qualifying surviving spouse, or a joint return, and it repealed the older rule that set the deduction at 15% of Maryland adjusted gross income between a floor and a ceiling. Section 10-217(c) then requires a cost-of-living adjustment for each tax year beginning after 2025-12-31, determined by the Comptroller, with the increase rounded down to the next lowest multiple of $50. So a 2026 amount exists in law, but Maryland has not published it: the Department of Legislative Services fiscal note for House Bill 411 of the 2026 session (First Reader, 2026-02-11) states that the 2026 amounts have not yet been announced, House Bill 411 itself died in committee, and the Comptroller has issued no 2026 figure since. This page therefore subtracts the 2025 statutory amounts and says so on the page. ABOUT $3,400, which is easy to mistake for the 2026 answer: the 2026 Maryland Employer Withholding Guide says that for the purpose of the percentage method calculation the Standard Deduction is $3,400, but that is an input an employer uses to work out withholding from a paycheck, and the guide prints that one figure above both of its rate tables, the joint and head of household table and the single table. The statute is not status-blind, it gives $3,350 to a single filer and $6,700 to a joint filer, so one all-status $3,400 cannot be the statutory per-status amount. Raising the single filer to $3,400 while leaving a joint filer at $6,700 would also apply the cost-of-living adjustment to one filing status only, which section 10-217(c) does not do. Head of household uses the joint bracket thresholds and the $6,700 deduction. Sources: Md. Code, Tax-General 10-217, https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Laws/StatuteText?article=gtg&section=10-217 ; House Bill 352 of 2025 as enrolled (Chapter 604), https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/2025RS/bills/hb/hb0352e.pdf ; fiscal note for House Bill 411 of 2026, https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/2026RS/fnotes/bil_0001/hb0411.pdf ; Comptroller of Maryland tax alert on the 2025 session changes to standard and itemized deductions, https://www.marylandcomptroller.gov/content/dam/mdcomp/tax/legal-publications/alerts/tax-alert-changes-to-standard-and-itemized-deductions-and-to-state-and-local-income-tax-rates-from-the-2025-legislative-session.pdf ; 2026 Maryland Employer Withholding Guide, https://www.marylandcomptroller.gov/content/dam/mdcomp/tax/instructions/withholding/2026/withholding-guide.pdf
disclaimer: Local income taxes are not included. Maryland counties and Baltimore City levy a separate LOCAL income tax (roughly 2.25%-3.30% of Maryland taxable income, varying by county) that is NOT included in this estimate. At moderate incomes the local piece can rival or exceed the state tax.

Maryland's tax rates for 2026 are current, but its standard deduction here is the 2025 amount, $3,350 for a single filer and $6,700 for a joint return or head of household. Maryland indexes the deduction to the cost of living for tax years after 2025 but has not announced the 2026 figure, so this page uses the 2025 one until it does.
The 2% Maryland surtax on net capital gains (for filers with federal AGI over $350,000) is not modeled.
Personal exemptions and itemized-deduction phase-outs are not modeled; this estimate assumes the standard deduction.
maryland.notes: Progressive 2%-6.5% (2026 statutory rates, incl. new 6.25%/6.5% high-income brackets). County/Baltimore City local income tax NOT included.

missouri.name: Missouri
missouri._source: Tax year 2026 Missouri brackets and standard deduction come from the Missouri Department of Revenue's 2026 Missouri Withholding Tax Formula and are confirmed by the tax rate chart on the 2026 Form MO-1040ES. Missouri applies one graduated schedule to every filing status: no tax on the first $1,348 of Missouri taxable income, then 2.0%, 2.5%, 3.0%, 3.5%, 4.0% and 4.5% in $1,348 steps, with the top rate of 4.7% on income over $9,436. Only the standard deduction changes with filing status, and for 2026 it matches the federal amounts: $16,100 single or married filing separate, $32,200 married when the spouse does not work, and $24,150 head of household. Separately from withholding, Section 143.171 RSMo still allows Missouri filers to deduct part of their federal income tax on the annual return. The deduction is a percentage of federal income tax liability set by Missouri adjusted gross income (35% at $25,000 or less, 25% from $25,001 to $50,000, 15% from $50,001 to $100,000, 5% from $100,001 to $125,000, 0% at $125,001 or more), capped at $5,000 per return or $10,000 on a married filing combined return, and it is claimed on Form MO-1040. Missouri's withholding formula does not apply it, so it does not affect your paycheck, and this paycheck estimate follows the withholding formula. Sources: https://dor.mo.gov/forms/Withholding%20Formula_2026.pdf , https://dor.mo.gov/forms/MO-1040ES_2026.pdf , https://revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=143.171
disclaimer: Local income taxes are not included. Missouri cities of Kansas City and St. Louis levy a separate 1% local earnings tax on wages, which is not included in this estimate.

Missouri's standard deduction conforms to the federal standard deduction. Not modeled here: the additional standard deduction for taxpayers age 65 or older or blind, the $1,400 additional exemption Missouri gives head of household and qualifying widow(er) filers on the annual return, and Missouri tax credits.

Missouri still lets you deduct part of your federal income tax when you file your annual return, under Section 143.171 RSMo. The deduction is a percentage of your federal income tax liability set by your Missouri adjusted gross income: 35% at $25,000 or less, 25% from $25,001 to $50,000, 15% from $50,001 to $100,000, 5% from $100,001 to $125,000, and 0% at $125,001 or more. It is capped at $5,000 per return, or $10,000 on a married filing combined return. Missouri's withholding formula does not apply this deduction, so it does not change your paycheck and this estimate leaves it out. Claim it on Form MO-1040 when you file.
missouri.notes: Progressive 0%-4.70% (official 2026 inflation-indexed brackets, top band over $9,436 of taxable income). Federal-conformed standard deduction. Separate 1% local earnings tax in Kansas City and St. Louis not included.

kansas.name: Kansas
kansas._source: Kansas tax year 2026 individual income tax: two-bracket schedule 5.20% / 5.58% enacted by Senate Bill 1 (June 2024 special session), which consolidated Kansas's prior three brackets (3.10% / 5.25% / 5.70%) into two and lowered the rates to 5.20% (taxable income up to $23,000 single/HoH, $46,000 married filing jointly) and 5.58% on income above those thresholds. Tax Foundation's 2026 state income tax data lists exactly these 2026 rates/thresholds for Kansas, and the standard deduction $3,605 single / $8,240 MFJ (HoH $6,180 per Kansas DOR). These statutory amounts are unchanged for 2026: SB269's conditional phase-down toward 4.0% only triggers if the state budget stabilization fund reaches 15% of the prior year balance, and that trigger did NOT lower the 2026 rates (Tax Foundation still lists 5.20%/5.58% for 2026). RESOLVED a conflict: one secondary source (LegalClarity) claims Kansas uses 3.10%/5.70% for 2026 with $30k/$60k thresholds — those are the PRE-REFORM legacy rates (3.1%/5.7% were the old bottom/top rates) mislabeled as current; rejected in favor of Tax Foundation 2026 + AARP + EY tax-news + WebSearch consensus on 5.20%/5.58%. Head of household uses the single $23,000 threshold with its own $6,180 standard deduction. https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/state/state-income-tax-rates-2026/ ; https://taxnews.ey.com/news/2025-1266-kansas-law-conditionally-lowers-personal-income-tax-rates-starting-in-2025
disclaimer: Kansas has no local/city income tax on wages.

Kansas grants a large personal exemption ($9,160 single / head of household, $18,320 married filing jointly, plus $2,320 per dependent) IN ADDITION to the standard deduction. This calculator models only the standard deduction, so for Kansas the estimated state tax will run HIGHER than actual for most filers (the personal exemption further reduces taxable income).
Kansas itemized deductions, tax credits (e.g. food sales tax credit, child/dependent care), and the additional standard deduction for filers age 65+ or blind are not modeled.
kansas.notes: Two-bracket 5.20% / 5.58% (Senate Bill 1, 2024; unchanged for 2026). Estimates run high because Kansas's separate personal exemption is not modeled. No local income tax.

arkansas.name: Arkansas
arkansas._source: Arkansas individual income tax for tax year 2026. The rates come from Act 1 of the First Extraordinary Session, 2026 (House Bill 1001, approved 5/6/2026), which amended Arkansas Code 26-51-201(a)(4) and lowered the top rate from 3.9% to 3.7% for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026. The statutory schedule is 0% up to $5,599, 2% to $11,199, 3% to $15,999, 3.4% to $26,399, and 3.7% from $26,400 to $94,700, and Arkansas applies the same schedule to every filing status. An identical companion measure, Act 2 of the same session (Senate Bill 1), was approved the same day. The standard deduction of $2,470 per taxpayer comes from the Arkansas Department of Finance and Administration Withholding Tax Formula Method, Tax Year 2026, effective 01/01/2026. Because the rate cut was signed in May 2026, that withholding booklet still prints the older 3.9% rate; the figures shown here follow the statute. Sources: Act 1 at https://www.arkleg.state.ar.us/Home/FTPDocument?path=%2FACTS%2F2026S1%2FPublic%2FACT1.pdf and the DFA 2026 withholding formula at https://www.dfa.arkansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/whformula_2026.pdf
disclaimer: Arkansas has no local or city income tax on wages.
Arkansas gives a $29 personal tax credit for each withholding exemption claimed on Form AR4EC, plus dependent credits. Those are not modeled here, so estimates run slightly high for most filers.

Once net taxable income passes $94,700, Arkansas phases out the benefit of the lower brackets, so the effective rate moves toward a flat 3.7% on all income. That taper is not modeled, so estimates above roughly $95,000 run modestly low.

Arkansas lowered its top rate to 3.7% in May 2026, backdated to January 1, 2026. Withholding tables printed before the cut still use 3.9%, so the tax actually taken out of your paycheck may be a little higher than shown here until your employer updates its tables.
arkansas.notes: Progressive 0% to 3.7% for tax year 2026. The top 3.7% rate begins at $26,400 of net taxable income. Arkansas uses the same rate schedule for every filing status; the standard deduction is $2,470 per taxpayer. No local or city income tax.

alabama.name: Alabama
alabama._source: Alabama individual income tax — statutory three-bracket schedule 2%/4%/5% under Ala. Code § 40-18-5, unchanged for 2026 (no rate change enacted; the 2%/4%/5% structure is long-standing and is the valid 2026 schedule), so figureYear=2026. Single/MFS/HoH thresholds: 2% to $500, 4% to $3,000, 5% above. Married-filing-jointly thresholds (exactly 2x single): 2% to $1,000, 4% to $6,000, 5% above. Confirmed across Tax Foundation 2026, halfpricesoft 2026, icalculator 2026, and AARP 2026 (identical brackets). Standard deduction modeled at the MAXIMUM amounts (single $3,000, MFJ $8,500, HoH $5,200, MFS $4,250), consensus across efile/halfpricesoft/icalculator/nationaltaxreports; the engine uses the max because Alabama's standard deduction is unusual — it is INCOME-PHASED (Standard Deduction Chart, Form 40), declining as Alabama AGI rises toward a lower floor that the engine cannot model. Validated rates vs Tax Foundation 2026 + halfpricesoft 2026 withholding tables. Hand-verified single $75k -> $3,560.00 exact (taxable = 75000-3000 = 72000; = 2%x500 + 4%x2500 + 5%x(72000-3000)). https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/state/state-income-tax-rates-2026/ ; https://www.revenue.alabama.gov/forms/standard-deduction-chart-40-3/
disclaimer: Alabama's standard deduction is income-based and PHASES DOWN as your Alabama AGI rises (from the maximums shown toward a lower floor); this estimate applies the maximum standard deduction, so for higher incomes the actual tax can be slightly HIGHER than shown.
Alabama's personal exemption ($1,500 single / $3,000 married / and $1,000 per dependent) and the dependent exemption are not modeled, so estimates run slightly high on that account.

Local income taxes are not included. Many Alabama municipalities/counties levy a separate LOCAL occupational (wage) tax (e.g. ~1% in Birmingham, Gadsden, Macon County) that is not included in this estimate.
The federal income tax deduction Alabama allows, and the 2026 overtime-pay subtraction (up to $1,000), are not modeled.
alabama.notes: Progressive 2%-5% (statutory, Ala. Code § 40-18-5), top 5% rate begins at just $3,000 taxable income (single) / $6,000 (married). Standard deduction is income-phased; max amounts modeled. Separate local occupational taxes apply in some cities.

south-carolina.name: South Carolina
south-carolina._source: South Carolina individual income tax — OFFICIAL South Carolina Dept. of Revenue guidance on H.4216 (Act 110, signed March 30, 2026), EFFECTIVE for tax year 2026 (returns due April 15, 2027). H.4216 REPLACES SC's old 0%/3%/6% three-bracket system entirely for TY2026 with a two-rate schedule on federal-AGI-based taxable income: 'the tax rate for income less than $30,000 is 1.99%' and 'the tax rate for income from $30,000 and above is 5.21%, minus $966.' The '5.21% minus $966' form is mathematically identical to a marginal two-bracket schedule (verified continuity at $30,000: 1.99% x 30000 = $597 = 5.21% x 30000 - 966), so modeled as marginal brackets: 1.99% to $30,000, 5.21% above — SAME rates for all filing statuses. SCDOR also created the new SC Income-Adjusted Deduction (SCIAD) replacing the federal standard/itemized deduction: $15,000 single/MFS, $22,500 head of household, $30,000 MFJ/surviving spouse (modeled as the standardDeduction). RESOLVED A GENUINE SOURCE CONFLICT: the Tax Foundation 2026 dataset still lists SC's OLD 0%/3%/6% system (top reverting to 6.2% on 7/1/2026) and federal std deduction $8,350/$16,700 — it predates H.4216, which was signed only March 30, 2026. The official SCDOR H.4216 page (ranked first per loop procedure) overrides the stale secondary, and PolicyEngine + ITEP corroborate the 1.99%/5.21% + SCIAD structure. figureYear=2026 (genuine official 2026 data, no prior-year fallback). Hand-verified single $75k -> $2,160.00 (taxable = 75000-15000 = 60000; = 1.99% x 30000 + 5.21% x 30000 = 597 + 1563). https://dor.sc.gov/news/information-about-h-4216 ; https://www.policyengine.org/us/south-carolina-2026-tax-changes
disclaimer: South Carolina rewrote its income tax for 2026 (H. 4216, Act 110): 1.99% on taxable income below $30,000 and 5.21% above, with the South Carolina Income Adjusted Deduction (SCIAD) replacing the federal standard deduction. The SCIAD starts at $15,000 for single or married filing separately, $22,500 for head of household and $30,000 for married filing jointly, and shrinks as income rises until it reaches zero at $95,000, $142,500 and $190,000 respectively. This calculator now applies that reduction. The statute measures it against your federal adjusted gross income; we use your wages less pre-tax deductions, so if you have income or adjustments outside your paycheck your real deduction may be smaller than shown.

South Carolina starts from federal AGI; this estimate approximates taxable income as wages minus the SCIAD and does not model federal-AGI adjustments, the capped state EITC ($200), or other SC credits.
South Carolina has no local/city income tax on wages.
Under H.4216 the top rate may be reduced further in future years if state revenue triggers are met; figures shown are the enacted 2026 rates.

Paycheck withholding is a separate calculation from the yearly tax. The 2026 SC Withholding Tax Formula the SC Department of Revenue currently publishes (form WH-1603F, Rev. 11/4/25) was issued before H. 4216 was signed and still withholds at the older 0%, 3% and 6% rates using a $5,000 personal allowance. Until the SCDOR reissues it, the South Carolina tax withheld on a 2026 paystub may not match the yearly estimate shown here.
south-carolina.notes: Two-rate 1.99% / 5.21% (H.4216 / Act 110, new for tax year 2026), 5.21% begins above $30,000 taxable income. New SC Income-Adjusted Deduction (SCIAD) replaces the federal standard deduction; it phases down with income. No local income tax.

rhode-island._source: Rhode Island individual income tax — 2026 inflation-adjusted figures. RI is a three-bracket graduated state (3.75% / 4.75% / 5.99%) with the SAME bracket schedule for ALL filing statuses (only the standard deduction varies); brackets are inflation-indexed annually and the 2026 amounts ARE officially published (figureYear=2026, no fallback). The official source is RI Division of Taxation Advisory 2025-22 (ADV 2025-22, issued 11/03/2025, 2026 inflation-adjusted personal income tax amounts) — its PDF on tax.ri.gov is Cloudflare/WAF-protected (HTTP 403 to automated fetch and a 'verify you are human' challenge in-browser, which I did NOT bypass), so the figures were taken from authoritative sources that publish ADV 2025-22 verbatim: the official advisory itself confirms the FIRST bracket reaches $82,050 (3.75%) and the standard-deduction/personal-exemption phase-out begins at MAGI $254,250; Tax Foundation 2026 supplies the full schedule and standard deduction: 3.75% to $82,050, 4.75% to $186,450, 5.99% above; standard deduction $11,200 single, $22,400 MFJ. HEAD-OF-HOUSEHOLD standard deduction ($16,800) is DERIVED from RI's documented statutory structure (HoH = single + half the single-to-MFJ gap = 11,200 + (22,400-11,200)/2), which reproduces RI's published prior-year HoH figure exactly (2024: 10,550 + (21,150-10,550)/2 = 15,850 = the reported 2024 HoH); it is the documented RI pattern, not a fabricated value, and is disclaimed as derived. SIMPLIFICATIONS (disclaimed, state-only): RI's standard deduction AND personal exemptions PHASE OUT entirely for modified AGI above $254,250 (fully eliminated by ~$287,050), which the engine cannot model — so estimates run LOW for high earners; personal exemptions (~$5,100/exemption) and RI credits are not modeled. Hand-verified single $75k -> $2,392.50 exact (taxable = 75000-11200 = 63800; entirely in the 3.75% band = 3.75% x 63800; engine returned 2392.50). https://news.bloombergtax.com/daily-tax-report-state/rhode-island-tax-division-announces-2026-inflation-adjusted-personal-income-tax-amounts ; https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/state/state-income-tax-rates-2026/
